vignette: Thomas is a 50-year-old European American male who works as a psychologist. He has been married for over two decades and recently sought help after experiencing significant distress following a traumatic rape incident that occurred several months ago. The event left him deeply shaken, with his symptoms gradually evolving into a debilitating pattern of avoidance and emotional numbing. The traumatic event itself was a harrowing experience. Thomas had attended a professional conference in the city, where he enjoyed a few drinks at an after-party. As he walked back to his hotel, feeling slightly disoriented from alcohol, he was attacked by someone who took advantage of his vulnerability. The fear and pain he experienced were overwhelming, leaving him with fragmented memories and deep emotional scars. Thomas reports that certain triggers, such as the smell of alcohol or the sound of sirens, have become potent reminders of this traumatic event. Whenever he smells alcohol, a flood of distressing emotions washes over him. The scent immediately transports him back to the moment he felt vulnerable and powerless. This experience has led Thomas to feel emotionally numb and disconnected from his surroundings. He finds it difficult to engage in activities that once brought him joy, such as socializing or attending professional gatherings where alcohol is present. The memory of the event itself remains elusive, making it hard for Thomas to fully process what happened. When he tries to recall specific details, he finds himself pushing the memories away before they can form a complete picture. This fragmented recollection exacerbates his negative appraisals about himself and his capabilities. He feels dehumanized, like an object rather than a person capable of agency and control. Thomas's sense of emotional numbness and self-deprecation are reinforced by these memory gaps. The inability to fully articulate or recall the traumatic event in detail has left him feeling that he is not capable of doing the things that once defined his identity as a psychologist. This cognitive dissonance further deepens his negative appraisals, leading to increased distress whenever he encounters triggers. In his daily life and work environment, Thomas finds it increasingly difficult to function professionally. He often avoids attending conferences or social events where alcohol is served, which has strained his relationships with colleagues and clients. His avoidance behaviors have led to a decline in his professional performance and interactions, further reinforcing his negative self-perceptions. Thomas's marriage has also been affected by these changes. He withdraws emotionally from his wife, finding it difficult to connect or engage in meaningful conversations. The fear of reliving the trauma through triggers and memory fragments makes him feel isolated and disconnected from those around him. What finally brought Thomas to seek help was a combination of professional burnout and emotional exhaustion. He realized that he could no longer maintain the facade of normalcy, especially as his symptoms began to interfere with both his personal relationships and work life. His primary fear is that he will never fully recover and reclaim the sense of self that once defined him. Thomas hopes for support in processing his trauma and regaining a sense of control over his life. Through this arc of experience, it becomes clear that Thomas's triggers amplify his negative appraisals, which in turn make it difficult to recall or articulate memories of the event. This cycle has gradually tightened around him, leaving him feeling trapped and disconnected from both himself and those around him.
